analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent the lower 15% capital gains tax rate and a larger, permanent estate tax exemption.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the House Ways and Means Committee and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would lock in the reduced capital gains tax rate of 15% that was scheduled to expire, so investment profits would never again be taxed at up to 20%. It would also rebuild the estate tax in a much lighter form: estates up to $3.75 million in 2010, rising to a permanent $5 million exemption (adjusted for inflation) by 2015, with lower tax rates above that, and a surviving spouse able to use any exemption the deceased spouse didn't use. Law outside these levels would see rates double on the largest estates above $25 million.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthiest households. The capital gains provision helps anyone with large investment gains, but the benefit scales with wealth because investment income is concentrated at the top. The estate tax provisions directly help families with multi-million-dollar estates, who would owe far less or nothing at death, and estate-planning professionals whose services depend on the rules.

how_it_helps.text: Makes permanent the reduced capital gains rate (15% instead of 20%) enacted in 2003, which was otherwise scheduled to expire [S2][S3].
Raises the estate tax exemption to $3.75 million in 2010, stepping up to a permanent $5 million by 2015, with inflation indexing after that [S2][S3].
Cuts estate tax rates: taxing estates at the capital gains rate up to $25 million and double that rate only above $25 million, with inflation adjustments after 2015 [S3].
Lets a surviving spouse use the unused portion of a deceased spouse's estate tax exemption, so a couple could shelter up to $10 million without complex trusts [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury. Every dollar of estate or capital gains tax not collected means higher deficits, other taxes, or less revenue for public services. Because the benefits go almost entirely to the wealthiest households, the cost falls on everyone else through the nation's finances. It also repeals the deduction for state death taxes after 2009, removing a small offset for estates subject to state inheritance taxes [S3].

drawbacks.text: The revenue cost would be large and would flow overwhelmingly to the wealthiest households, since capital gains and taxable estates are heavily concentrated at the top of the income and wealth distributions.
The bill repeals the deduction for state death taxes for decedents dying after 2009, which would slightly increase the total tax on the largest estates in states with their own death taxes [S3].

Critics of permanent low capital gains rates argue the preferential rate encourages holding assets for tax reasons rather than productive reasons and gives the largest an advantage over wage earners, whose income is taxed at ordinary rates. This is a general policy objection, not drawn from the bill text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but narrowly distributed: permanent certainty for investors and a simpler, lighter estate tax for multi-million-dollar families, including sensible portability of a spouse's unused exemption. The cost is a permanent reduction in federal revenue that everyone else indirectly bears. The design is coherent, but the incidence is lopsided toward the very wealthy.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Harry Mitchell (D-AZ) introduced the bill on July 24, 2007, joined by Rep. Christopher Shays (R-CT) [S1][S3][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
The only further action was the sponsor's introductory remarks in the Congressional Record on July 25, 2007 [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal treasury and, indirectly, everyone else: the scheduled expiration of the capital gains cut and the pre-2010 estate tax rules were never overridden, so no additional revenue was permanently forgone.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal treasury kept the revenue

for.name: Rep. Harry E. Mitchell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chair: Rep. Charles Rangel, D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred; no hearing, markup, or report, so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with one Republican and one Democratic cosponsor, and it died quietly in committee without any vote that would have revealed a partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would permanently cut capital gains rates and raise the estate tax exemption to $5 million, benefits that scale directly with wealth. The cost shows up as federal revenue that others must eventually make up.

A permanent, inflation-indexed $5 million exemption with spousal portability would reshape estate planning for wealthy clients, creating new work around portability elections while simplifying some planning. Its interest tracks its clients, not the general public.
Making the 15% capital gains rate permanent would give high-net-worth clients a permanent reason to hold assets for the preferential rate, supporting fee-generating assets under management.
